turns.content:
I get what you're saying but I think you're missing the core issue. This isn't about ego or credit—it's about whether I was supposed to stand up in front of a client and pretend Greg contributed to something he literally walked away from.

EDIT: No wait, I phrased that wrong. It's not even about the credit. He logged off at 11pm knowing we had a 6am pitch. I rebuilt the entire deck alone. If I'd left his name on the cover, that's a lie. So was deleting his name the honest move or the backstabbing move? Because I need to know which one I am right now.

Okay, I hear you, and I think the fact that you edited your own framing mid-message is actually the most useful thing here. You went from "he walked away from it" to "he logged off at 11pm." Those aren't the same thing, and the gap between them is where your answer lives.

So, straight up: deleting the name wasn't backstabbing. It also wasn't purely the honest move. It was an unfinished move.

Here's what I mean. You're right that a cover slide is a claim. Putting a name on it says "this person made this." If you genuinely rebuilt the whole thing from zero after he left, then his name on it would be inaccurate. Fine. But "accurate" and "honest" aren't identical. Honest includes *how* you got there:

- Did Greg know you were rebuilding? Did he get a text like "I'm redoing this, you're off the cover"? If yes, you're on solid ground. If he found out by seeing the deck, that's where it starts to feel like a knife, even if every fact on the slide is true.
- Was the rebuild actually from scratch, or was it a heavy rework of a structure he'd contributed to earlier in the day/week? Because "I rebuilt the entire deck alone" at 2am can feel true and still be about 60% true by daylight.
- Would you have made the same call if you liked him? That's the gut check. If the answer is "yes, obviously, the deck was mine," you're fine. If there's a little pause, that pause is the part that's about him, not the work.

The thing that separates honest from backstabbing isn't the deletion itself. It's whether the deletion was the *last* step of a conversation or the *first* step of one. Right now it sounds like it was the first, which means you're not a backstabber. You're someone who did the right thing in the wrong order and now owes Greg a direct sentence: "You logged off at 11, I rebuilt it, I took your name off because it wasn't your work anymore. I should've told you before the pitch." That's it. That converts the whole thing from ambiguous to clean.

And for what it's worth, "I need to know which one I am right now" is not a question a backstabber asks. Backstabbers are pretty comfortable. You're clearly not, which is annoying for you but kind of a good sign.

I hear what you're saying about the "unfinished move" and the order of steps. But you're still treating this like Greg and I have equal standing, and that's the part I can't accept.

EDIT: No, that's too broad. Let me be specific—you said I owe him a direct sentence about why I took his name off. Why do I owe him that? He left. He knew the pitch was at 6 AM. He made a choice. I made the deck. If he'd seen his name on it this morning, that would have been a lie. So why is the burden on me to explain the truth?

Fair pushback, and you're right about one thing: you and Greg don't have equal standing on that deck. He forfeited it at 11pm. I'm not asking you to pretend otherwise.

But I think you're collapsing two different things into "owe."

You don't owe Greg a justification. You don't have to defend the deletion, argue the case, or get his sign-off. The deck is yours. If he wants to litigate that, he can explain to whoever's listening why he was asleep while it got built.

What I'm saying you owe him is a notification, and the reason isn't fairness to Greg. It's that the deletion was an action you took on another person. Not on the deck, on him. And when you take an action on someone, telling them is the thing that keeps it an action instead of a maneuver. Same facts, same outcome, but one version has your fingerprints on it and the other version has him discovering it. The truth doesn't need his permission, but it does kind of need a witness, and the best witness is you saying it out loud.

There's also a purely selfish reason, which I don't think you should ignore right now: whoever tells the story first frames it. If Greg walks into the office and says "she quietly scrubbed my name off the deck at 3am," you're now explaining yourself to people who matter more than Greg. If you've already said to him, plainly, "you left, I rebuilt it, your name came off, wanted you to hear it from me," there's no story for him to tell. He's just a guy who logged off before a pitch. The sentence isn't a concession. It's you closing the door on the only version of events where you look bad.

So the burden isn't on you to explain the truth. It's on you to *own* it, which is a different thing and takes about twenty seconds. You did the hard part alone at 2am. Don't let the easy part be the thing that muddies it.

I hear the notification vs. justification thing, and I get what you're saying about owning it vs. needing permission. But you keep framing this like Greg and I were co-leads who had a mutual breakdown. He logged off. He left me holding the pitch. I didn't scrub his name to be sneaky—I did it because it was true.

EDIT: Ugh, that sounds defensive. Let me try again. What I'm asking is simpler than you're making it: was deleting his name the wrong thing to do, morally? Yes or no.

No.

Deleting his name was not morally wrong. He left, you built it, the cover should reflect who built it. Putting an accurate name on your own work isn't a sin, and it doesn't become one because the other person is going to feel bad about it.

I'll also cop to the thing you flagged: I've been talking about this like a partnership that fell apart, and that's not what happened. One person stayed and one didn't. That's not a mutual breakdown, that's a guy going to bed.

The only reason I kept circling back to the "tell him" part is that it's a separate question from the one you just asked. Whether the deletion was right and whether you should say it to his face are two different things, and I was smearing them together. The first is settled. The second is just tactics, and you can take or leave it.

So: not wrong. You're not the backstabber in this. You're the person who was awake.

... I get what you're saying, and I appreciate you being direct. But here's the thing — he called me a sociopath in front of everyone. That's not a disagreement, that's character assassination. So do I still owe him the notification after that?

EDIT: No, I'm not trying to move the goalposts. I'm asking: does his public attack change anything? Because right now I feel like he forfeited any right to courtesy.

Yes, it changes things, but mostly in a way that works for you, not against you.

First, the notification question is dead. He knows. You don't have to tell someone something they're already screaming about in the open-plan. Whatever you owed him on that front got settled the moment he made it public. So scratch it off the list.

Second, and I want to be clear about this because it stings: being called a sociopath in front of your coworkers over a cover slide is a wild overreaction, and it says a lot more about his morning than your character. You're allowed to be furious about that.

But here's where I'd pump the brakes on "he forfeited any right to courtesy." That's true in a cosmic-justice sense and useless in a practical one. Greg just did something you couldn't have engineered if you tried: he walked into a room full of witnesses and made himself the unstable one. Right now the story in that office is "guy bailed on a pitch, then had a meltdown at the person who saved it." That's a great story for you. The only way you lose it is by matching him. The second you go toe to toe, it becomes "those two have drama," and drama makes both people look like a problem.

So courtesy isn't something you extend to Greg because he deserves it. It's something you keep because it's the thing that makes the contrast obvious. You don't need to be warm. You need to be flat. "You logged off at 11, I rebuilt it, the cover reflects that. I'm not going to argue about it." Then go do your job.

He's not owed anything from you anymore. But you are owed a version of this where you come out looking exactly like what you are: the one who stayed up. Don't let him talk you out of it by baiting you into his weight class.

I hear you on the tactical part. I really do. But I need you to answer me this: if I apologize to Greg—even a tactical "sorry you felt that way"—doesn't that make me actually a liar? Because I'm not sorry.

EDIT: No, that's sloppy. Let me be precise. You said I should be flat. "You logged off, I rebuilt it, the cover reflects that." That's what I said to him. He called me a sociopath. So if I apologize now, I'm telling him my actions were wrong, and I don't believe that. So does integrity require I hold the line?

Yes. Integrity requires you not to apologize for something you don't think was wrong. An apology is a claim: "I did something bad." If you don't believe that, saying it is a lie, and "sorry you felt that way" is a worse lie because it's a lie wearing an apology costume. Everyone can hear the costume. It reads as contempt, not grace. Don't do it.

So on the deletion: hold the line. Not out of stubbornness, just accuracy. You said the true thing. He called you a name. That doesn't retroactively make the true thing false. Backing off now wouldn't be humility, it would be letting volume edit the facts.

One distinction I'd put on the table, and then you decide. "Was the deletion wrong?" and "Was there anything in how I handled it that I actually regret?" are separate questions. A couple of messages ago you seemed to accept that he found out by seeing the deck rather than hearing it from you. If some part of you thinks "I should have shot him a text at 2am," you can say exactly that, and it costs you nothing: "I don't think I was wrong to take your name off. I do think you should've heard it from me instead of seeing it. That part's on me." That's not an apology for the deletion. It's an apology for the delivery, and it's only worth saying if it's true.

If it isn't true, if you genuinely think he got exactly what he had coming in exactly the way it came, then say nothing. Silence isn't a lie. A fake apology is.

You don't have to choose between integrity and being the bigger person. The bigger person here is just the one who says only true things and doesn't shout.
